cards.name: Neon tube glow
cards.summary: Type reads as a lit neon tube: a pale hot core, a saturated coloured rim and a soft halo of the same colour bleeding onto a dark wall.
use_for: night-life, gaming and event headlines on dark backgrounds
thumbnail words that must glow off a dark frame
avoid: light or white backgrounds: the halo disappears; use an outline or a shadow instead
long body copy: the glow fills the counters of small letters
print without raising Effect > Document Raster Effects Settings to 300 ppi in Illustrator: the glows are raster effects and come out coarse

cards.name: 3D extruded block type
cards.summary: Headline letters get solid depth: side walls run back from each letter in a darker shade of the face colour, like chunky 3D signage.
use_for: poster and thumbnail headlines that must pop
avoid: long text: each letter's walls overlap its neighbours; keep to a few words
Photoshop alone: it has no 3D in this version; build the type in Illustrator or CorelDRAW and place it, or use the shallow stacked-shadow stand-in below
Illustrator Revolve (Classic): its scripted apply drew nothing

steps.note: On the type (fill = face colour, stroke = a darker shade: the verified render showed stroked shapes' walls take the stroke colour). Rotation keys are radians: -0.2 / -0.45 is a gentle three-quarter view; depth in pt.
Optional: Object > Expand Appearance to hand off flat art (the 3D render becomes an image plus paths).

Extrude on the artistic text: Small Back toward a vanishing point locked to the page (VPType 1, document inches), placed below right of the text; Depth 70; colour shading from a mid red to near black on the side walls.

cards.name: Flat long-shadow type
cards.summary: A hard-edged diagonal shadow runs from every letter out to the edge of the panel and fades away, the flat-design long shadow on headline type.
use_for: flat poster and social headlines on solid colour
avoid: photos or busy backgrounds: the shadow shape fights them
thin script fonts: the sweep turns into a mess of slivers
a soft realistic shadow: use a normal drop shadow

steps.note: Create Outlines, then copy the outlines behind (Paste in Back) and fill the copy with the shadow colour.
On the shadow copy: 200 copies, each 1 pt further along the diagonal. The vertical sign is not confirmed: if the copies climb, use moveV_Pts -1.
Bake the copies into paths.

Group the copies first: on the overlap plate re-render Add gave one outline-free silhouette in the topmost object's paint (identical to the Effect menu); check it on screen, then Expand Appearance again.
Shadow at 20-30 % opacity in Multiply over the panel colour (pageItem.blendingMode = BlendModes.MULTIPLY).
Clip the shadow with a copy of the background panel so it stops at the edge.

Extrude, Back Parallel with one solid side colour. For a parallel extrusion the page-locked vanishing point (VPType 1) fixes the run: the walls end where the point is, 6.5 in right and 6.5 in down from the text centre here (a 45 degree sweep that leaves the panel at the bottom edge).

steps.script:
groups = [layer.Shapes.Item(i) for i in range(1, layer.Shapes.Count + 1) if layer.Shapes.Item(i).Type == 11]
result = groups[0]
steps.note: Selects the extrusion group (the walls the effect added behind the text) so the next two steps act on it, not on the text.
Break Apart on the selected extrusion group turns the live effect into plain curves: a group of the 14 wall faces.

Weld (script): the Weld menu item on the broken-apart group kept only part of the faces (the G and D shadows were dropped in a first run), so the script ungroups the 14 faces and welds them one after another with Shape.Weld into one shadow shape, then puts it behind the text. The shadow now runs from all three letters.
steps.script:
g = [layer.Shapes.Item(i) for i in range(1, layer.Shapes.Count + 1) if layer.Shapes.Item(i).Type == 7][0]
g.UngroupAll()
faces = [layer.Shapes.Item(i) for i in range(1, layer.Shapes.Count + 1) if layer.Shapes.Item(i).Type == 3]
print('faces', len(faces))
w = faces[0]
for f in faces[1:]:
    w = f.Weld(w, False, False)
w.OrderBackOf(labels['type'])
print('welded', w.Type, round(w.SizeWidth,2), round(w.SizeHeight,2))
result = w

steps.note: Linear fountain transparency on the welded shadow: opaque at the letters, clear at the far end (mid point 40, so the fade starts early), angle along the 45 degree sweep. The shadow reaches the corner of the panel almost clear.

steps.note: Layer > Duplicate Layer (new first step, target 'type'; 'LONG' in Arial Black 360 px, white on a #F2C14E panel): ran, 'LONG copy' (labelled 'shadow') sits above the type layer.
Layer > Rasterize > Type on the duplicate (target 'shadow'): ran, the copy is now an ordinary pixel layer.

Script (target 'shadow'): the rasterised copy is moved below the type layer and merged onto a black layer, so it is white letters on black ('ramp'). Nine times the ramp is duplicated, moved 1, 2, 4 ... 256 px down-right, darkened to 99.5 % ^ that distance of full white (Levels output) and merged back in Lighten mode, so each pixel keeps the brightest copy: a diagonal run of 511 px whose brightness falls with distance from the nearest letter edge (about 8 % left at the far end). The ramp's luminosity is then loaded as a selection and a new layer 'long shadow' is filled with #1F3A4D through it, below the type, and the ramp is deleted. Ran in about 25 s. This replaces the first run's 100 copies (about a minute) and the Gradient Overlay: the shadow now fades per letter, one pixel step at a time, with no stair-stepping and no end cap, and runs off the bottom and right of the panel. The recipe's Color / Gradient Overlay steps are not used.
